A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MVC-ZigAL research. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and qualitative figures, support a reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original finetuning experiments, quantitative comparisons, ablations and generated multiview images, including additional analyses in its appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds larger-training and SDXL finetuning experiments. Its original results are distinguishable from baseline results attributed to MATE-3D.

M1.justification: The central architecture, zigzag sampler and optimization objectives remain. However, Algorithm 1 changes the reported update order: v1 constructs mixed rewards before updating the Lagrange multiplier, whereas v2 uses the updated multiplier. v2 also specifies trajectory resampling within an inner optimization loop; these procedural revisions do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: Both versions cover the animal prompt set, MATE-3D's diverse 160 prompts and the retained qualitative prompt sets. v2 reuses MATE-3D for training and adds backbone configurations, but introduces no new dataset, generation task or test domain; those changes concern experimental settings.

E2.justification: v2 Table 4 adds SPAD, Latent-NeRF and TextMesh to the MATE-3D comparison and removes its standalone MV-ZigAL rows. Table 2 adds the non-finetuned baseline and MV-ZigAL to the ablation comparison. Figures 8–11 substantially expand visual comparisons with competing methods; the MV-PG/MV-DPO/MV-RDL comparison remains.

E3.justification: v2 adds MATE-3D training for 100 epochs with larger batches and a lower learning rate, plus 16-step SDXL finetuning with LoRA rank 4. Table 2 specifies epoch-70 checkpoints for all finetuned variants, whereas v1 documents 190 epochs for MV-ZigAL and 70 for MVC-ZigAL. No held-out split is documented for the added MATE-3D training experiment.

E4.justification: Appendices F–G add analyses of training-scale effects and applicability to SDXL, including reward trajectories in Figure 7. Existing zigzag, weighted-sum, adaptive-threshold and adaptive-step-size ablations are retained. Figures 5–6 move from the appendices into the main text rather than introducing new ablations.

E5.justification: Both versions specify seed 42 and use the same seed for qualitative comparisons. Neither reports repeated-run variability, confidence intervals or significance tests. v2's additional result rows and training curves do not introduce a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Table 1 and standard MVC-ZigAL benchmark scores remain unchanged. v2 adds HyperScore submetrics, comparator results, SDXL curves and larger-training results, including 8-step HyperScore 7.24 and ImageReward 0.865. MV-ZigAL's 8-step HyperScore is 6.95 in the new epoch-70 comparison versus 7.33 previously, not an established same-setting decline. Reported DreamFusion and Consistent3D scores also change from 4.15 to 4.13 and 4.21 to 4.08.

T1.justification: The Lagrangian formulation, advantage losses and inversion equations are retained, with v1 Appendix F largely incorporated into the main text. However, v2 Equation (2) assigns terminal reward at t=0 while defining actions as x_(t-1), unlike v1 Equation (8)'s consistent terminal transition. This introduces a limited formal indexing inconsistency rather than new theory.

C1.justification: v2 adds an explicit central claim that clustered rewards in few-step generation produce weak learning signals and that structured self-refinement advantages address this problem. It more clearly presents MV-PG, MV-DPO and MV-RDL as baselines. The main contributions concerning multiview coordination, constrained optimization and preserved inference efficiency remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of zigzag refinement as filtering condition-misaligned features and producing more informative learning signals. Appendices F–G interpret the added experiments as evidence of scalability and broader backbone applicability. The existing first-step structural explanation, reward trade-off interpretation and approximate-inversion caveat remain.

D1.justification: v2 Table 3 documents hyperparameters for the added larger-training and SDXL configurations, and Appendix C expands the optimization-loop description. Conversely, it omits v1's RTX 4090 identification, 22–24-hour runtime, dedicated MV-ZigAL hyperparameter block and Table 1's 192-image averaging detail. The paper's code link remains the same.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to constrained policy optimization, Latent-NeRF, TextMesh and constrained-RL diffusion alignment, while removing the original language-model DPO reference. Appendix A's positioning relative to multiview generation and alignment methods is largely retained. Publication updates to existing references do not constitute new related work.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and much of the method narrative are extensively rewritten. v2 separates baseline formulations from MVC-ZigAL, moves detailed T2I preliminaries into Appendix B, incorporates the constrained-objective derivation into the main text and moves adaptive-optimization analyses into the main ablation section.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main layout, moves Figure 1 onto the opening page, restructures comparison and hyperparameter tables, and adds Figures 7–11. Existing adaptive-optimization plots move into the main text. v1's final five qualitative figures are retained as v2 Figures 12–16, rather than being new results.

improvement.justification: The added SPAD comparison, metric breakdowns, SDXL experiments and clearer organization provide useful gains. However, Table 4 labels evaluations out-of-distribution while including a model trained on the same MATE-3D prompts without a documented held-out split. Unlike v1's pseudocode, v2 Algorithm 1 averages joint rewards after zero-mean normalization, which would eliminate the stated constraint-feedback signal. These gains and new methodological reporting problems prevent a reliable net quality judgment.
